subject: Science
theme: lithium-ion battery cathode composition and material distribution
question_short_text: Which three of four elements usually make up EV battery cathodes?
text:
In the context of electric vehicle batteries, consider the following elements:

I. Cobalt
II. Graphite
III. Lithium
IV. Nickel

How many of the above usually make up battery cathodes?
explanation: Cobalt, lithium, and nickel are the three elements that typically compose EV battery cathodes. Graphite is not used in cathodes; it is the standard anode material in lithium-ion batteries.

research.summary:
The key insight here is understanding the functional separation between cathode and anode in lithium-ion batteries, and the specific roles of each element. In modern EV batteries, the cathode contains multiple elements organized as metal oxide compounds, while the anode remains fundamentally different in composition.

Lithium is the foundational active element in all cathode chemistries—it forms compounds like lithium cobalt oxide (LiCoO₂), lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide (LiNiMnCoO₂, commonly NMC), and lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO₄, or LFP). Lithium ions shuttle between cathode and anode during charging and discharging, making this element essential to battery function.

Cobalt enhances cathode stability and energy density. It appears in chemistries like lithium cobalt oxide and NMC/NCA formulations. However, due to cost and supply concerns from the Democratic Republic of Congo, the industry is gradually reducing cobalt content—some next-generation cathodes use significantly less cobalt or omit it entirely.

Nickel is increasingly critical in modern EV cathodes because it increases energy density and extends driving range. Nickel-based chemistries (NMC and NCA, which stands for Nickel-Cobalt-Aluminum) accounted for 80% of battery capacity deployed in new EVs in 2021 and are now the dominant choice for long-range vehicles.

Graphite is the critical material for the anode, not the cathode. It comprises the entire anode in lithium-ion batteries and is valued for its electrical conductivity, low cost, and stable structure. This is the main trap in the question—students often confuse all four materials as interchangeable battery components when in fact graphite belongs to a completely different electrode.

The practical takeaway: most modern EV batteries rely on one of two cathode chemistries. NMC (Nickel-Manganese-Cobalt) was the dominant chemistry in 2020, but NCA (Nickel-Cobalt-Aluminum) is also common in high-performance EVs. Meanwhile, the emerging alternative is LFP, which uses iron and phosphate instead of cobalt and nickel, yet still requires lithium. In every single case, lithium is present, but the other transition metals vary. Graphite remains exclusively an anode material.
facts: NMC (Nickel Manganese Cobalt) batteries accounted for 72% of EV batteries globally in 2020 and remain dominant due to their balance of energy density, power, and safety.
Nickel-based cathodes (NMC and NCA) represented 80% of battery capacity deployed in new plug-in EVs in 2021, reflecting the industry shift toward higher nickel content to reduce cobalt dependence.
Graphite comprises the entire anode in standard lithium-ion batteries and is the single-largest mineral component by weight, not a cathode material.

Cobalt content in future cathodes is projected to fall significantly (from ~200 g/kg to ~60 g/kg of cell weight) as manufacturers develop low-cobalt and cobalt-free chemistries to address cost and supply chain risks.

Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) is an emerging alternative cathode chemistry that uses iron and phosphate instead of cobalt and nickel, yet still requires lithium, showing that lithium is the only universal cathode element among the four options.
